definition: Having or showing very strong and sincere feeling about something.
example: My grandfather stayed a fervent admirer of old jazz records long after his friends lost interest.
nuance: Fervent suggests warm, sincere intensity; fervid often hints at overheated excess, and zealous can imply fanatical action.
prompt: A volunteer describes the community garden she started on an empty lot.
options: Her fervent belief in shared green space kept her weeding there every weekend for years.
She was so fervent about the garden that she rarely bothered to visit it.
The fervent soil in the lot produced twice as many tomatoes as last summer.
She gave a fervent, half-hearted wave when neighbors asked about the plants.
reasons: Years of steady effort grow naturally out of an intense, heartfelt conviction.
Ignoring a project shows indifference, the reverse of passionate feeling.
This confuses the word with fertile; dirt can be rich but cannot feel passion.
A half-hearted gesture lacks the strong emotion the word requires.

practice.prompt: Supporters of a small-town soccer team attend the championship final.
options: The fervent supporters left at halftime because they found the match boring.
The fervent referee calmly applied every rule without favoring either side.
The fervent grass on the field had been mowed into neat stripes before kickoff.
The fervent supporters sang through the second half even while their team trailed.
reasons: Walking out from boredom shows a lack of feeling, not an abundance of it.
Calm neutrality is admirable for a referee but is the opposite of strong emotion.
Grass has no emotions, so it cannot be passionate about anything.
Singing loudly despite losing shows intense, sincere devotion.
